body:
Why the Mansabdari System Was Important

Akbar ruled an expanding empire that needed military commanders, civil officials and nobles loyal to the central authority. The mansabdari system provided a common method of ranking these officers, determining their remuneration and assigning military responsibilities.

Mansab and mansabdar

Mansab means a position or rank. A mansabdar was an imperial officer holding such a rank. The system covered both military and civil service and was developed into an important administrative institution under Akbar.

Mansabdars came from different backgrounds, including Turanis, Iranis, Afghans, Indian Muslims, Rajputs and other groups. Their inclusion helped the empire combine different regional elites within a common structure of imperial service.

The Difference Between Zat and Sawar

Mansab ranks came to be expressed through two numerical components: zat and sawar. They measured different aspects of an officer's position.

  • Zat: The officer's personal rank and standing in the imperial hierarchy. It was an important basis for determining personal salary. An officer with a higher zat generally ranked above an officer with a lower zat.
  • Sawar: The officer's cavalry responsibility. It indicated the number of mounted soldiers the officer was required to maintain under the terms of the appointment.

Understanding a rank

Suppose one mansabdar held 3,000 zat and 1,000 sawar, while another held 2,000 zat and 1,500 sawar. The first officer had the higher personal rank because his zat was higher. The second had the larger stated cavalry obligation because his sawar was higher.

The Mughal administration sought to check military obligations through inspection and registration of cavalrymen and branding of horses. The purpose was to verify that officers maintained the military resources for which they received remuneration.

How Mansabdars Were Paid

Holding a mansab did not mean that an officer automatically became the owner of a territory. The emperor could remunerate mansabdars in different ways.

  • Cash payment or naqdi: Some officers received salaries directly in money.
  • Jagir: Many officers received an assignment of the right to collect specified revenue from a territory. This revenue was intended to support their remuneration and obligations.

Jagir and jagirdar

A jagir was a revenue assignment, not an outright transfer of ownership of all land within the assigned territory. A jagirdar was the person holding the assignment. The jagirdar generally obtained revenue rights rather than independent sovereignty over the territory.

Most mansabdars did not reside in or personally administer their jagirs. Revenue could be collected through their representatives, while the mansabdars performed imperial duties elsewhere.

Ordinary salary jagirs were generally transferable. The ruler could reassign them, which helped prevent officials from treating imperial appointments as independent hereditary kingdoms. There were exceptions, particularly the hereditary and non-transferable watan jagirs associated with the hereditary territories of certain Rajput ruling houses.

Jagir and Khalisa: An Important Distinction

Jagir lands were assigned for the remuneration of officers. Khalisa lands, by contrast, provided revenue directly to the imperial treasury rather than being assigned as an officer's jagir.

Problems in the Later Mansabdari System

Under Akbar, jagir assignments were generally assessed with the intention that their estimated revenue would correspond approximately to an officer's salary. However, the amount expected from a jagir could differ from the amount actually collected.

During Aurangzeb's reign, the number of mansabdars increased while the supply of satisfactory jagir assignments became more difficult to manage. Some officers received assignments whose actual collections were below their expected remuneration. Others waited for assignments.

These difficulties encouraged some jagirdars to press cultivators for higher collections during the limited period of their assignment. Such pressure contributed to rural discontent and weakened the effectiveness of imperial administration.

Prelims focus

  • Mansab: Official rank; mansabdar: holder of that rank.
  • Zat: Personal status and salary rank.
  • Sawar: Cavalry responsibility.
  • Jagir: Assignment of revenue rights, not ownership of the entire assigned territory.
  • Khalisa: Revenue reserved for the imperial treasury.
  • Trap: A higher sawar figure does not by itself establish a higher personal rank; zat determines that distinction.

[NCERT, Our Pasts – II, Class 7, Chapter 4, The Mughal Empire, pp. 51–52; NCERT, Themes in Indian History – Part II, Class 12, Theme 8, Peasants, Zamindars and the State, p. 214; NIOS, Senior Secondary History (315), Lesson 12, Administrative System and Institutions, section 12.11, Mansab System, consulted 19 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Zat determined personal rank; sawar indicated cavalry responsibility.

title: Mansabdari and Jagirdari: Rank, Military Service and Revenue Assignments

body:
Why Land Revenue Mattered

Land revenue was the principal financial foundation of the Mughal Empire. The government needed revenue to maintain the army, pay officers and support administration. Because agricultural production differed from one locality to another, the state required information about cultivated land, crops and their value.

Raja Todar Mal, Akbar's revenue minister, played an important role in organising land revenue assessment. The system associated with his work sought to make assessments more systematic and predictable in areas where detailed measurement and record-keeping were possible.

What Was Zabt?

Zabt was a Mughal land revenue assessment system in which cultivated land and crop information were used to determine revenue demand according to established cash rates. Its successful operation depended on adequate surveys and careful revenue records.

During Akbar's reign, information on crop yields, prices and cultivated areas over a 10-year period, 1570–1580, was used in fixing revenue assessments. The resulting revenue rates varied according to the crops cultivated and the revenue schedules applicable in different areas.

The underlying principle was to establish a revenue demand using recorded agricultural conditions rather than requiring every official to negotiate an entirely new assessment without reference to past information.

Basic Stages of Assessment and Collection

  1. Survey cultivated land: Establish the extent of agricultural land where measurement is feasible.
  2. Record agricultural information: Use information about the crops grown, their yields and prevailing prices.
  3. Determine the revenue demand: Fix a crop-wise assessment using the applicable cash rates.
  4. Collect the revenue: Revenue officials and local intermediaries seek to realise the assessed amount from cultivators.

The process distinguished between deciding what was due and obtaining what was actually paid. The two did not always produce the same amount.

Jama and Hasil

Two terms are particularly important for understanding Mughal revenue administration:

  • Jama: The amount of revenue assessed or officially expected.
  • Hasil: The amount of revenue actually collected.

For example, if the assessed demand from an area was 1,000 units of money but officials actually collected 800, the jama would be 1,000 and the hasil would be 800. These are illustrative figures, not historical revenue statistics.

The difference mattered because mansabdars receiving jagirs were often remunerated according to an expected revenue value. When actual collections were lower than the assessed amount, an officer's real income could be below expectations.

Cash Assessment and Payment in Kind

Under zabt, revenue demand was expressed using cash rates. However, this does not mean that every cultivator throughout the Mughal Empire invariably paid every assessment in coins. Mughal revenue administration also allowed collection in kind under certain arrangements.

It is therefore important to distinguish assessment in monetary terms from the form in which payment was actually made. Crop-sharing and other methods of collection existed alongside more standardised cash assessments.

Where Zabt Could Not Be Applied Uniformly

Zabt depended on the ability of officials to survey land and maintain accurate accounts. It was not equally feasible in every part of the empire.

The Gujarat and Bengal exception

NCERT identifies Gujarat and Bengal as provinces where the detailed surveying and accounting required for zabt could not be carried out in the same manner. This does not mean that these provinces were exempt from Mughal revenue demands. It means the particular zabt method could not be uniformly applied there.

The difference shows why a large empire could have a broadly common administrative structure while using varied revenue practices according to local conditions.

Who Were the Zamindars?

The term zamindar covered different types of local intermediaries, ranging from village headmen to powerful regional chiefs. Many helped connect the imperial revenue administration with the cultivators who produced agricultural goods.

Zamindars did not necessarily own all the land cultivated by the peasants under their influence. Their authority could arise from local rights, established positions and political power. Some cooperated with Mughal officials, while others resisted imperial demands, sometimes with the support of cultivators.

Prelims focus

  • Todar Mal: Revenue minister associated with Akbar's land revenue reforms.
  • Zabt: Crop-wise cash revenue assessment based on systematic records.
  • 1570–1580: The 10-year period of agricultural information used for Akbar's assessment.
  • Jama: Assessed revenue; hasil: Revenue actually collected.
  • Gujarat and Bengal: Examples where the detailed zabt survey system was not uniformly feasible.
  • Trap: Inability to apply zabt uniformly did not mean that a province paid no land revenue.

[NCERT, Our Pasts – II, Class 7, Chapter 4, The Mughal Empire, pp. 52–53; NCERT, Themes in Indian History – Part II, Class 12, Theme 8, Peasants, Zamindars and the State, pp. 213–215; NIOS, Senior Secondary History (315), Lesson 12, Administrative System and Institutions, sections on Mughal revenue administration, consulted 19 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Cultivators harvest wheat in a Mughal village while officials measure a field with rope and a record keeper writes on paper.
pictures.caption: Measuring cultivated land and estimating produce were central to Mughal revenue assessment.

pictures.alt: Agricultural records inform zabt rates and jama of 1,000 units; actual hasil is 800 units. Gujarat and Bengal were not uniformly suitable for detailed surveys.

title: Akbar's Land Revenue System: Zabt, Todar Mal and Regional Differences

body:
Why Relations with Rajput Rulers Mattered

The Rajputs controlled important kingdoms, forts and military resources, particularly in Rajasthan. For an expanding Mughal Empire, durable authority required more than defeating regional rulers in battle. It also required securing their cooperation or reaching settlements that reduced repeated warfare.

Akbar developed a policy that combined military campaigns, matrimonial alliances, imperial appointments and political accommodation. Different Rajput states responded differently. Consequently, Akbar's Rajput policy should not be understood as either complete friendship with all Rajputs or continuous war against every Rajput kingdom.

Cooperation with Amber

Amber, ruled by the Kachhwaha Rajputs, became an important Mughal ally. In 1562, Akbar established a matrimonial alliance with the ruling family of Raja Bharmal of Amber.

The alliance was politically significant. Rajput nobles could enter Mughal service, receive high mansab ranks and command imperial forces. In return, the emperor obtained experienced military and political supporters who understood regional conditions.

Raja Man Singh of Amber became one of Akbar's prominent commanders. His position illustrates that Rajput nobles could serve as leading officers in the Mughal military system rather than merely remaining subordinate rulers in their home territories.

Resistance from the Sisodiyas of Mewar

The Sisodiya rulers of Mewar resisted Mughal supremacy for a prolonged period. Akbar captured Chittor in 1568, but this victory did not bring an immediate end to resistance throughout Mewar.

After Rana Udai Singh, Maharana Pratap continued opposition to Mughal authority. The best-known military encounter of this phase was the Battle of Haldighati in 1576.

  • Mewar's side: Led by Maharana Pratap.
  • Mughal side: Led by Raja Man Singh of Amber, acting as a commander of Akbar's forces.
  • Result: The Mughal forces gained the advantage in the battle, but Maharana Pratap escaped and resistance in Mewar continued.

Who commanded at Haldighati?

Haldighati was fought during Akbar's reign, but Akbar did not personally command the Mughal army on the battlefield. Raja Man Singh was the principal Mughal commander opposing Maharana Pratap.

Political Accommodation and Watan Jagirs

Akbar's policy also sought to incorporate regional ruling houses without necessarily removing their established local positions. Rajput chiefs who accepted Mughal supremacy could receive imperial ranks and revenue assignments.

A watan jagir was an assignment associated with a ruler's hereditary homeland. Unlike ordinary transferable salary jagirs, watan jagirs were hereditary and non-transferable and were connected to the established rights and territories of particular ruling families.

This arrangement made political accommodation more attractive: a Rajput ruler could acknowledge the emperor's supremacy and participate in imperial service while retaining important local ties.

Settlement with Mewar under Jahangir

The prolonged conflict with Mewar was settled during Jahangir's reign in 1615, when Amar Singh of Mewar accepted a political settlement with the Mughal emperor.

The timing is important. Akbar's capture of Chittor in 1568 and the Battle of Haldighati in 1576 were followed by continued resistance. The later settlement in 1615 occurred under Jahangir, not Akbar.

Political Effect of Akbar's Rajput Policy

The Rajput policy helped Akbar expand imperial authority while obtaining the service of experienced regional elites. It also shows the limits of conquest: rulers who were defeated could continue resistance, while negotiated settlements sometimes achieved stability more effectively than repeated campaigns.

The policy was not applied with identical outcomes everywhere. The cooperation of Amber and the resistance of Mewar are the principal examples that demonstrate this distinction.

Prelims focus

  • Amber: Kachhwaha Rajput kingdom allied with Akbar; matrimonial alliance in 1562.
  • Raja Man Singh: Important Rajput commander in Mughal service.
  • Chittor, 1568: Captured by Akbar.
  • Haldighati, 1576: Maharana Pratap opposed Mughal forces commanded by Raja Man Singh.
  • 1615: Settlement with Amar Singh of Mewar under Jahangir.
  • Trap: The Battle of Khanwa involved Rana Sanga in 1527; Haldighati involved Maharana Pratap in 1576.

[NCERT, Our Pasts – II, Class 7, Chapter 4, The Mughal Empire, pp. 49–51; NIOS, Senior Secondary History (315), Lesson 10, Establishment of the Mughal Rule, section 10.4, consulted 19 November 2026; NIOS, Military History (375), Chapter 8, section 8.3, The Battle of Haldighati, consulted 19 November 2026; IGNOU, unit on Mughal relations with Mewar, section on the 1615 settlement, consulted 19 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Amber allied with Akbar in 1562; Mewar resisted after Chittor and Haldighati, reaching settlement under Jahangir in 1615.
pictures.caption: Amber's cooperation and Mewar's prolonged resistance followed different courses.

title: Akbar's Rajput Policy: Alliances, Resistance and Political Accommodation
